title: Settlement Economy: production, consumption and trade of goods
about: The design: the statement (statement.md) as elements, each quoting its text, and the decisions that refine it. plan.json implements it: every feature names the design elements it serves, and tools/check_plan.py reports any element no feature serves.
source: statement.md (verbatim from the user, prompt M16 in requests.json)
summary: Resources stop being map tokens that a civilization either has or lacks. They become **goods measured in physical quantities**: tonnes of wheat, dairy and coal, bales of cotton, crates of arms. Each settlement **produces** goods from the land it works, its improvements, its buildings, its specialists and its population. It **consumes** them in proportion to its size and way of life. Surpluses and shortages drive growth, contentment, industry, trade and war. Diplomacy moves from leasing a resource for gold per turn to **real commerce**: shipping goods, selling seeds and breeding stock, and negotiating multi-part contracts.

elements.text: 1. **Physical quantities.** Every good is counted in units that mean something (tonnes, bales, barrels, crates) and is conserved: it is made, moved, stored, used up or spoiled. Nothing appears from nowhere.

2. **Production comes from the whole settlement.** Output combines worked tiles and their improvements, buildings, specialists and available labour. Land sets what is possible; people and capital set how much of it is realised.
3. **Consumption comes from population.** A settlement of a given size needs a plausible amount of food, fuel, clothing and comforts. Needs rise with size and with era.
4. **Industry transforms goods.** Factories turn inputs into outputs at defined rates, and the scarcest input limits the result.
5. **Military power has a material cost.** Units are built from production and goods, and armies in the field use supplies.
6. **Trade carries the goods themselves.** Civilizations exchange goods, the means to produce them (seeds, livestock, techniques), money and treaties, in deals of any shape.
7. **The simulation lives in the DLL.** The game's rules run in the DLL; XML holds the data and Python shows it to the player.
**Today's resource types become entries in this catalogue.** No good sits on a map plot.
**Tiles:** the land's qualities for that good (climate, soil, ore grade, fishing grounds), times the improvement built on the tile.
**Labour:** citizens working tiles produce raw goods. Specialists produce specific goods or multiply buildings' output, for example a miller, a smith or an engineer.
processing (a mill makes flour; a dairy turns milk into cheese and butter);
storage (granary, warehouse);
industry (foundry, textile mill, arsenal).
**Technology and policy:** multipliers on yields, and new production methods.

**Effects of being supplied:** a need that is met adds to growth, health and contentment, with diminishing returns. A shortfall causes hunger, illness, unrest and lost production. Larger settlements need proportionally more, so a single shipment of coffee no longer satisfies an empire.
**Stocks** sit in the settlement and are limited by its storage buildings. Perishable goods (fish, dairy, fruit) decay unless preserved.
**Within a trade network,** surpluses flow to shortages automatically, limited by roads, rivers, ports and harbours. A blockade or a cut road changes what reaches a city.
**Recipes:** buildings convert inputs into outputs at set rates and capacities. For example, 2 iron ore and 1 coal make 2 steel; 1 steel and 1 sulphur make 1 crate of arms.
**Units** cost production plus goods, such as muskets, horses, steel and fuel. In later eras, armies in the field draw supplies, so industrial capacity and supply lines become part of warfare.
| Goods | 50 tonnes of wheat; 10 crates of arms; coffee | Physical: shipped and used up |
| Means of production | Coffee seeds, breeding cattle, silkworms, mining or brewing techniques | Knowledge or stock: the buyer can then produce it |
| Money | Lump sum, instalments | Financial |
| Agreements | Open borders, alliances, rights to fishing grounds, exclusivity clauses | Political |
**Spot deals:** one shipment, delivered now.
**Supply contracts:** a quantity per turn for a set term at an agreed price, with penalties for failing to deliver.
**Packages:** any combination. For example: 20 tonnes of grain per turn for 30 turns, plus coffee seeds, in exchange for iron ore, open borders and a lump sum.
**Delivery is physical.** Goods travel by land or sea routes. Distance, ports and blockades affect what arrives, and war can break contracts.
The AI values a good by its **marginal value**: what one more unit changes in its own settlements' growth, contentment and output.
Gold is valued at what it can buy.
It also weighs the strategic cost of giving a rival the means to produce a good, for example selling seeds versus selling the harvest.
Prices come from supply and demand among trading partners. That rewards monopolies, specialisation and stockpiling, and lets the player see why a good is valuable.
**XML:** the goods catalogue, needs per citizen, building recipes and capacities, specialist outputs, and unit costs.
**Python:** the settlement goods screen, trade and contract views, and map overlays of land qualities.

**The bridge to the existing engine:** a settlement that is supplied with a good also holds the matching resource count. That keeps existing building requirements, the AI and the trade screen working while the new systems are built. I checked in the code that a city's resource count reaches its trade network.

decisions.question: Scale of units
decisions.choice: Real quantities in whole integers, each good in its own unit (tonnes, bales, barrels, crates), sized so no value can overflow; never shown as a fulfilment ratio.

decisions.question: Food
decisions.choice: Staple food is a good in tonnes. A city eats first and grows from its surplus; citizens starve only when stores are empty. Spoilage of food depends on the preservation technologies the owner lacks.

decisions.question: Number of goods
decisions.choice: The game's existing resource types, plus three new goods: Timber (from lumber camps and lumbermills on forest), Dairy (from cow and sheep pastures) and Leather (from horse, cow and sheep pastures).

decisions.question: Need tiers
decisions.choice: Needs grow along two building chains the game already has. The essentials buildings (Settlement, Town, City, Metropolitan) set how much a citizen needs of the basics (staple food, fuel, clothing). The market chain (Market, Fair, Commodity Market, Commercial Center, Hypermarket) sets which further goods a citizen wants and how much (variety, comforts, luxuries). Technological progression raises output through the techs' existing yield changes.

decisions.question: Distribution
decisions.choice: As the game works now: goods are shared across a connected trade network (CvPlotGroup: roads, rivers, coast). Blockades count: enemy ships blockading water plots take them out of the network (CvUnit::updatePlunder, CvPlot::isTradeNetwork), which changes what reaches a city and what deliveries arrive. Transport limits apply only to units (their cargo), not to goods.

decisions.question: Contracts and the trade screen
decisions.choice: Modify the executable's diplomacy screen through the DLL (item list and item text); no separate trade screen.

decisions.question: Order of work
decisions.choice: Geography and the way tiles work first (component LQ), then the goods accounts and production.

decisions.question: Icons
decisions.choice: Every good keeps its icon; no icon is missing or shared. New goods get their own button, art define and glyph in both font atlases (GameFont.tga, GameFont_75.tga), made with the repository's art studio (tools/civ4-art-studio) from realistic photographic textures whose licence allows use in the mod; the source and licence of each image are recorded.

decisions.question: Wool
decisions.why: Nothing places, gives or uses BONUS_WOOL today (catalogue.json), yet clothing needs it
decisions.choice: Sheep pastures yield wool, beside meat, dairy and leather.

decisions.question: Resources that are not physical goods
options: outside the goods accounts: Drama, Music, Movies stay building-given resources; Ancient Temple and Thermal Vent stay map sites
decisions.why: They are culture given by buildings or sites with no improvement that trades them (catalogue.json)

decisions.question: Fuel before coal
decisions.why: No timber or wood resource exists; the existing fuel goods are coal, oil, uranium, diesel, methane, biofuel and whale (catalogue.json)
decisions.choice: Timber is the fuel before coal: the fuel need applies from the start, met by timber, then coal, then oil.

decisions.question: Clothing in the early game
decisions.why: These are the only existing clothing goods (catalogue.json)
decisions.choice: The clothing goods are wool, leather, fur and cotton.
decisions.source: follows from R1 (wool and leather added)

compared_with_today:
| | Today | Proposed |
|---|---|---|
| Resource | A token on one tile; you have it or you don't | A quantity, produced and used up |
| Source | The one tile holding the token | Tiles, improvements, buildings, specialists, labour |
| Demand | None; one copy serves every city | Each settlement uses goods in proportion to its size |
| Luxury | +1 happiness per city, whatever its size | Contentment that grows with supply per head |
| Industry | Buildings need inputs present and use nothing | Buildings convert inputs into outputs |
| Units | Need a resource present | Cost goods; armies use supplies |
| Diplomacy | Lease a resource for gold per turn | Shipments, seeds, contracts, packages |
